drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: White wanted you to grab the a3 pawn, because after Qxa3 your queen leaves d3 and Qxf5 and Qxb4 come in while Rc1 gets ready to hit your queen. You were sitting on +7.3, and that pawn grab hands White the activity he needs. Qxd1 is the move: after Qxf7+ Kxf7 Rxd1 the queens are gone and you finish roughly a rook up for a pawn. The principle is to cash in a loose rook before you chase a wing pawn.
drills.threat: Your queen on d3 is staring at White's rook on d1, which is defended only once, by the rook on e1.

drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: White wanted to win that bishop outright with Nxh4 or Qxh4. Retreating to f6 gives up the better option, because Bxf2+ takes the pawn with check and the bishop can then go after the Re1, so after Kh1 and Bxe1 Rxe1 you have traded your bishop for a rook. Instead, Bf6 lets Ng5 offer a trade and f4 gains space while White's queen gets active, and you were at +6.8 and throwing that edge away. The principle is to check whether a capture with check is the escape you were looking for.
drills.threat: White's knight on f3 and queen on h5 both attack your bishop on h4, and the f2 pawn behind it is guarded only by the king.

drills.coachNote: White wanted to chase your queen off the c-file with tempo and then pick up the c7 pawn. Qb6 keeps c7 defended, but Nf5 forces Rd7, Qc3 takes over the long diagonal, and you end up pushed back to g6 with nothing to do. You were level at 0.0 and this costs about four pawns of value. Qe3 steps off the file and hits the d3 pawn and the loose knight on g3 at once, and in the line Qxc7 Qxd3+ you win the pawn back with check. The principle is to move the queen to a square that attacks something concrete, not one that only feels safe.
drills.threat: White's rook on c1 is looking straight down the open c-file at your queen on c5, and nothing defends that queen.

drills.coachNote: White wanted dxc4 to win your pawn and bring Ng3 into the fight while your queen sits passively. The principle is that when a pawn attacks yours and it is your move, capturing it first is usually right.

drills.coachNote: Qb3 looks like a fix because it adds a defender along the third rank and hits the knight on b4, but the defence is hollow. After Bxd3 you cannot recapture with the queen, since Nxd3 wins her, and the line Nxa7 Kxa7 Qxb4 leaves you a bishop down for a pawn. You were at +0.7, and that one move throws away about four pawns of value. Rc7 is the answer: it hits the queen on d7 with the rook and forces the trades that clear d3 on your terms. The principle is to check whether your defender survives the recapture before you believe a piece is safe.
drills.threat: Black's knight on b4 and bishop on g6 both aim at your bishop on d3, which only your queen on d1 defends.

drills.coachNote: Black wants to trade on f4 and open lines for his d6 bishop, and the retreat to h2 gives him exactly that: Bxh2+ Kxh2 is a trade you didn't need, and after Kb8 your Ne5 only arrives with a tempo on the queen on d7. You were at +4.6, and stepping back along the same diagonal hands back the initiative worth about 3.6 pawns. Nb5 is the move, because it attacks the bishop on d6 and the a7 and c7 pawns while your bishop stays where it is. The engine line Bxf4 Nxa7+ Kc7 exf4 Bxd3 shows how the knight keeps Black busy. The principle is to challenge an attacker with a new threat rather than retreat along the line it is already on.
drills.threat: Black's bishop on d6 is aimed straight at your bishop on f4, which is defended only by the e3 pawn.

drills.coachNote: White wants Rb8+ while your king sits on d8, because Nc8 is then forced and the d6 and e6 pawns roll on. Kd8 looks sensible since it guards the knight on e7, but it walks onto the rank the rook is aiming at, and Rb8+ Nc8 c6 Rh7 leaves you passive while the pawns advance. Kc8 keeps the check harmless, since Rb8+ simply runs into Kxb8. The engine line still gives up the knight after c6 and Bc4 dxe7, so you're picking the less bad option, but Kd8 cost you about eight pawns from a position already at -2.7. Before you put your king on a rank, count which checks the rook has.

drills.coachNote: White's plan is Rxc5 with check, since your king on c8 shares the c-file with his rook, and then the rook gets to c8 while e6+ follows. Kd7 steps off the file, but it doesn't defend c5 and lets White's e6+ come with tempo, so the pawn falls and your king gets chased. Nxd5 is stronger because it takes the d5 pawn while the knight also covers c7 and b6, which keeps the king's squares under control. After Rxc5+ Rc7 is forced, and the rooks come off on c6, so you trade one pawn for another. Grab material that doesn't drag your king into the checking lines.

drills.coachNote: Your queen on c6 lines up on g2 and your rook on f2 is already guarding that square, so the king on g1 has no escape. Rxb2 grabs a pawn but pulls that rook off f2, removing the support that made the mate work. Once g2 is unprotected, Nd2 gives White's king some air, and the attack fizzles into a grab of the d3 pawn with Qxd3. Qg2 is mate because the king can't take the queen and has no squares on f1 or h2. At +20 you were winning by a mile, and you gave the forced mate away for a pawn on b2. Before you grab material, check whether the mate is already on the board.
drills.threat: White's queen on g5 is eyeing your bishop on e5, but his king on g1 is the real target for your queen and rook.

The line continues Re1 Bd6 a4, and the bishop retreats to a safe square. a6 cost you about 1.7 pawns of evaluation, so ask which of your pieces is loose before you spend a move on a pawn.

Bxf5 settles the question: exf5 recaptures, but Qd7 hits f5 at once, so White's pawn structure is under pressure and the knight that was annoying you has been traded for your bishop. b6 cost you about 1.4 pawns of evaluation from a position that was already slightly in your favour. drills.coachNote: White's job is to push the e-pawn while keeping Black's king off the f-file, so your king has to escort the pawn rather than wander. Kf4 walks onto the f-file, where Black can answer Kf7 with tempo, and after e4 Ke7 Ke3 your king has arrived late, costing you about ten pawns from a position at +19.8. The engine prefers Kf3, which keeps the king ready to support e4 and reach e3 without giving Black the f-file. You were winning by a mile, so the danger was the move order, not the position. In pawn endings, count how many moves your king needs to stand where it supports the pawn before you move it.

Bb3 spends a tempo on a bishop move that does nothing for that race, and after Ke7 Kc4 Kf7 you've gained no ground while Black's king settles in. Ba2 is the cleaner move, and the engine line Ke7 Kc4 Ke8 Kb5 Kd8 shows your king reaching b5 beside Black's queenside pawns while his king is still stuck on the back rank. You were at +19.8 and this costs about ten pawns' worth, so in king endings the king's route to the pawns matters more than the bishop's shuffles.

drills.coachNote: Black's rook and queen are aimed at d2, and Qxd2 is mate: the rook guards d2 along the second rank so your king can't take, and every escape square is covered. Rf1 leaves the knight defended only by your king and adds nothing against that attack, so Qxd2# comes immediately. You were at +5.6 with a winning attack, and that move throws the game away on the spot. Qd7+ comes first with check, forcing Black's king to move, and then O-O-O puts your rook on d1 so the knight is defended twice while your king leaves the e-file. Carry this forward: before any quiet move, find which of your pieces has only one defender and count the attackers lined up behind it.

Qg6+ attacks the king on e8 along the g6-e8 diagonal and the rook on h5 at the same time. After Kd7 Qxh5 the rook falls, and Black's king is still on the wrong side of the board. drills.coachNote: White wants b6 and b7 with the a6 pawn guarding that square, and your king is too far away to help, so the rook has to do the stopping. Rc4+ looks active, but the check lets White's king step to d5 and attack the rook, so after Kd5 the rook gets chased to c3 and the pawn keeps running. You were already behind at -7.4, and this costs another four pawns. Rc1 keeps the rook on the back rank, where it can drop to b1 and attack the pawn from behind: after b7 Re1+ Kd5 Rb1 the rook is in the fight for the pawn. Carry this forward: a rook behind a passed pawn is the most efficient blockade, and a check is only worth it if the king ends up somewhere worse.

Rc7 looks like it covers the seventh rank, but after b6 your rook is a tempo short of the b-file: Rc1 b7 Ra1 and the pawn has already arrived on b7. You were already behind at -6.5, and this costs about three more pawns. Ra7 attacks the a6 pawn directly, which ties White's rook to defending it instead of supporting the push, and the rook still covers b7 along the seventh rank. Carry this forward: against an advancing pawn chain, put your rook on the square that attacks the front pawn, not the one that waits for the next step.

Carry this forward: in a pawn ending your king is your strongest piece, so don't walk it away from the pawns it's guarding.

You were at +58.2, and this throws away almost fifty pawns' worth of that edge. Rb2 takes the rook out of the king's reach at once, onto the second rank where it stays active, and the line Ka3 Bg4 Rh2 Kc6 shows it swinging to the h-file while your king heads for c6. Qh7 puts your queen in the way of White's queen, and Qxh7+ Kxh7 forces a queen trade that takes the back-rank danger off the board, with Bf4 Re8 Rxe8 to follow. Carry this forward: when a rook you're using as a guard is the only piece covering a back-rank square, check whether moving it opens a mate before you move it.

Rxf6 removes the bishop that holds the whole attack together. Qxf6+ Rg7 Qxc6 then costs you a rook for a bishop, but it survives the attack, and that's the trade to accept. drills.coachNote: White wanted e5, the push that attacks your knight on f6 and cramps your kingside. Nbd7 was the developing move that let it happen, because it spent your tempo on the queenside while the e5 push went unchallenged. After e5 Ne8 Qe2 f6 your knight is pushed backwards and your position is tied up, so the 2.5-pawn swing takes you from +1.0 to about -1.5. The answer is e5 yourself, striking the d4 pawn first, and after dxe5 Ng4 the knight hits the e5 pawn while Qf4 Qe7 Nf3 completes the trade. Carry this forward: when your opponent prepares a pawn push against your knight, count the squares that knight has before you commit another piece.
drills.threat: White's e4 pawn is ready to push to e5, hitting your knight on f6 and leaving it no good square.

drills.explanation: Nd2 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Rac1 ran into Qxe4, costing about 4.5 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs Nixerleet (559) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black wanted Qxe4, grabbing the knight on e4, which nothing defends because your queen on e2 is blocked by your own e3 pawn. Rac1 was a quiet rook move that let it happen, and it left the knight in the crossfire of Black's queen. After Qxe4 you are a full piece down, and the 4.5-pawn swing takes you from level at +0.3 to about -4. Nd2 is the answer: the knight retreats to a square where it stays in play, and after Rd8 Nf3 you hit the bishop on e5 with tempo, with the line continuing Kg7 Qc2 Rd6. Carry this forward: before any quiet move, list your pieces that are attacked and undefended, because an unguarded knight is a gift.
drills.threat: Black's queen on c6 is eyeing your knight on e4, which has no defender at all.

drills.explanation: Re2 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, Rxe3 left that piece hanging: after Qxe3+ it's simply lost.
drills.title: vs Nixerleet (559) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black wanted e2, and the pawn on e3 is already a monster with the queen and rook lined up behind it. Rxe3 grabs the pawn, but Qxe3+ comes with check on the e3-g1 diagonal, you must recapture with the queen, and Rxe3 takes your queen. You have given a rook and queen for a queen and a pawn, a 2.4-pawn swing from a position already at -6.8. Re2 blockades: the rook sits on e2 in front of the pawn, so it cannot advance, and the line runs Qd5 Qf4 Qg5+ Qxg5 Bxg5 with the queen trade killing Black's attack. Carry this forward: when an enemy passed pawn is deep, blockade it with a piece in front before you grab material.
drills.threat: Black's pawn on e3 is pushing toward e2 and the first rank, backed by the queen on e4 and rook on e8.

drills.explanation: g6 was the move — it keeps your pieces coordinated and avoids the tactic that punished your game move. In the game, h6 ran into Bxf6, costing about 3.0 pawns of advantage.
drills.title: vs AnusCarlsen69420 (485) — Caro Kann Defense Advance Variation
drills.coachNote: White's idea is Bxf6 exf6, followed by Qh5+ with check straight down the h5-e8 diagonal at your king. Your h6 push is what let it happen, because it pulls the h-pawn off the square where it could help, so after Qh5+ the g6 block is nearly forced and you are left with doubled f-pawns and a weakened shield. The 3.0-pawn swing drags you from -0.8 to nearly -4. The answer is g6 right now, blocking the diagonal before the queen arrives, and after Bd3 Bg7 O-O the bishop sits behind the g6 pawn on the long diagonal, with Nbd7 and Nf3 to follow. Carry this forward: when a check is brewing on a diagonal, put a pawn on the blocking square and back it with a bishop rather than spending a tempo on the rim.
drills.threat: White's bishop on g5 wants to trade off your knight on f6, clearing the way for the queen to swing onto h5.
